questions.explanation: The longest chain has 4 carbons (a butene) and the double bond starts at carbon 1 (counting from the end nearest the double bond), so it is named but-1-ene.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the IUPAC name of the simplest alkyne, with molecular formula C2H2?
questions.explanation: Alkynes contain at least one carbon-carbon triple bond and take the suffix '-yne'; the two-carbon member is ethyne (commonly called acetylene).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which functional group is characteristic of the alkanols (alcohols)?
questions.explanation: Alkanols are identified by a hydroxyl group, -OH, attached to a saturated carbon chain, as in ethanol, CH3CH2OH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which functional group is characteristic of the alkanoic acids (carboxylic acids)?
questions.explanation: The carboxyl group, -COOH, gives alkanoic acids their characteristic weak acidity, as seen in ethanoic (acetic) acid, CH3COOH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which functional group is characteristic of the alkanoates (esters)?
questions.explanation: Esters (alkanoates) contain the -COO- linkage formed when the -OH of a carboxylic acid condenses with the -OH of an alcohol, releasing water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which functional group is characteristic of the amines?
questions.explanation: Amines contain an amino group, -NH2, derived formally from ammonia, and behave as weak bases because of the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Amines behave as weak bases mainly because
options: the nitrogen atom has a lone pair of electrons that can accept a proton
they contain a hydroxyl group that releases OH-
they are strongly acidic in aqueous solution
questions.explanation: The lone pair on the nitrogen of an amine can accept a proton (H+) from water or an acid, forming an alkylammonium ion, which is the basis of their weak basic character.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Structural isomerism occurs when two or more compounds
options: have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements of atoms
are simply different physical states of the same compound
have the same structural formula but different molecular masses
questions.explanation: Structural isomers share an identical molecular formula (same numbers of each type of atom) but differ in how those atoms are bonded together or arranged.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Butane, C4H10, has a straight-chain structural isomer and a branched-chain structural isomer. What is the IUPAC name of its branched-chain isomer?
questions.explanation: C4H10 exists as straight-chain butane and as its branched isomer, 2-methylpropane (also called isobutane), both sharing the molecular formula C4H10 but differing in carbon skeleton arrangement.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Fractional distillation is used to separate crude oil into useful fractions such as petrol, kerosene, and diesel, based mainly on differences in
options: boiling point of the hydrocarbon components
density of the hydrocarbon components only
solubility of the hydrocarbon components in water
questions.explanation: Crude oil is heated and passed up a fractionating column with a temperature gradient; each fraction condenses out at the height corresponding to its characteristic range of boiling points.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Cracking of large hydrocarbon molecules from crude oil is carried out mainly to
options: convert less useful, high-boiling-point hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful alkanes and alkenes
combine small hydrocarbon molecules into larger ones
separate crude oil into its fractions by boiling point
remove sulphur impurities from crude oil
questions.explanation: Cracking uses heat and/or a catalyst to break carbon-carbon bonds in large hydrocarbon molecules, producing a mixture of smaller, more commercially useful alkanes and alkenes.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In addition polymerisation, such as the formation of poly(ethene) from ethene monomers, the reaction proceeds
options: only in the presence of a strong acid catalyst
only between two different types of monomer
by monomers joining across their carbon-carbon double bonds, with no small by-product molecule formed
by monomers joining with the loss of a small molecule such as water at each linkage
questions.explanation: Addition polymerisation opens up the C=C double bonds of unsaturated monomers, allowing them to link directly together without releasing any by-product, unlike condensation polymerisation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In condensation polymerisation, such as the formation of a polyester (terylene) or nylon, the reaction proceeds
options: only using monomers that contain a carbon-carbon triple bond
by monomers joining together with the elimination of a small molecule, typically water, at each linkage
by monomers simply adding across carbon-carbon double bonds
without any chemical reaction between the monomer units
questions.explanation: Condensation polymerisation joins monomers bearing two reactive functional groups (such as -COOH and -OH, or -COOH and -NH2), releasing a small molecule (usually water) at every new linkage formed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Saponification is the process in which
options: an alkanol reacts with an alkanoic acid to form an ester and water
an ester (fat or oil) is hydrolysed by a hot concentrated alkali to form soap (a sodium or potassium salt of a fatty acid) and glycerol
a carbonate reacts with a dilute acid to release carbon dioxide
an alkene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst
questions.explanation: Saponification is alkaline hydrolysis of a triglyceride ester (fat/oil), breaking the ester linkages to yield soap (the fatty acid salt) and glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) as by-products.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Esterification is the reaction between an alkanoic acid and an alkanol, catalysed by concentrated sulphuric acid, to produce
questions.explanation: Esterification is a condensation reaction: alkanoic acid + alkanol -(conc. H2SO4)-> ester + water, e.g. ethanoic acid + ethanol -> ethyl ethanoate + water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the name of the ester formed from the reaction between ethanoic acid and ethanol?
questions.explanation: Ester names combine the alcohol-derived part (ethyl, from ethanol) with the acid-derived part (ethanoate, from ethanoic acid), giving ethyl ethanoate, CH3COOC2H5.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Volumetric analysis is a quantitative technique that determines the concentration of a solution by
options: measuring the electrical conductivity of the solution
measuring the volume of a solution of known concentration that exactly reacts with a measured volume of the solution being analysed
measuring the volume of gas evolved from a reaction
weighing the mass of a solid precipitate formed
questions.explanation: Volumetric analysis (titration) uses a standard solution of known concentration added from a burette until the reaction with a measured volume of the unknown solution is exactly complete, as shown by an indicator.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In a titration between a strong acid and a strong base, a suitable indicator would be
options: either methyl orange or phenolphthalein, since both change colour sharply within the steep pH range of the equivalence point
no indicator is required at all
only universal indicator, since it must show a numerical pH value
questions.explanation: A strong acid-strong base titration has a very steep pH jump near the equivalence point (roughly pH 4 to pH 10), so both methyl orange and phenolphthalein change colour sharply within that range.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In a titration between a weak acid and a strong base, the most suitable indicator to use is
options: litmus, since it changes colour gradually over a wide pH range
starch, since it only detects iodine
phenolphthalein, since the equivalence point occurs on the alkaline side of pH 7
methyl orange, since the equivalence point occurs on the acidic side of pH 7
questions.explanation: For a weak acid-strong base titration, the salt formed is slightly alkaline at the equivalence point, so phenolphthalein (which changes colour in the alkaline pH range, about 8.2-10) is the appropriate indicator.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: In a titration between a strong acid and a weak base, the most suitable indicator to use is
options: methyl orange, since the equivalence point occurs on the acidic side of pH 7
no indicator can be used with a weak base
phenolphthalein, since the equivalence point occurs on the alkaline side of pH 7
universal indicator, since only it can be used with weak bases
questions.explanation: With a strong acid and a weak base, the salt formed is slightly acidic at the equivalence point, so methyl orange (which changes colour in the acidic pH range, about 3.1-4.4) is the appropriate indicator.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: 20 cm3 of a NaOH solution of unknown concentration exactly neutralises 25 cm3 of 0.05 mol/dm3 H2SO4. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH solution. (H2SO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O)
questions.explanation: Moles of H2SO4 = 0.025 dm3 x 0.05 mol/dm3 = 0.00125 mol. Since the mole ratio of acid to base is 1:2, moles of NaOH = 2 x 0.00125 = 0.0025 mol. Concentration of NaOH = 0.0025 mol / 0.020 dm3 = 0.125 mol/dm3.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: 4.6 g of a monobasic acid, HA, is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm3 of solution. A 25 cm3 portion of this solution requires 20 cm3 of 0.25 mol/dm3 NaOH for complete neutralisation (HA + NaOH -> NaA + H2O). Calculate the molar mass of the acid.
questions.explanation: Moles NaOH used = 0.020 dm3 x 0.25 mol/dm3 = 0.005 mol = moles of acid in the 25 cm3 portion (1:1 ratio). Moles of acid in the full 250 cm3 = 0.005 x 10 = 0.05 mol. Molar mass = mass/moles = 4.6 g / 0.05 mol = 92 g/mol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: 2.86 g of hydrated sodium trioxocarbonate(IV), Na2CO3.xH2O, is dissolved and made up to 250 cm3 of solution. A 25 cm3 portion requires 20 cm3 of 0.1 mol/dm3 HCl for complete reaction (Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2). Calculate the value of x. (Na2CO3 = 106, H2O = 18)
questions.explanation: Moles HCl in aliquot = 0.020 x 0.1 = 0.002 mol. Moles Na2CO3 in aliquot = 0.002/2 = 0.001 mol. Moles in the full 250 cm3 = 0.001 x 10 = 0.01 mol. Molar mass of hydrate = 2.86 g / 0.01 mol = 286 g/mol. Mass of water = 286 - 106 = 180 g, so x = 180/18 = 10, giving Na2CO3.10H2O.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Adding sodium hydroxide solution dropwise, then in excess, to a solution containing Fe2+ ions produces
options: a green precipitate that is insoluble in excess NaOH
a reddish-brown precipitate that is insoluble in excess NaOH
a white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH
questions.explanation: Fe2+ ions form a dirty green gelatinous precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide with NaOH, which does not dissolve even when excess NaOH is added.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Adding sodium hydroxide solution to a solution containing Fe3+ ions produces
options: a white precipitate that is soluble in excess NaOH
a blue precipitate that is soluble in excess NaOH
a reddish-brown precipitate that is insoluble in excess NaOH
a green precipitate that is insoluble in excess NaOH
questions.explanation: Fe3+ ions give a reddish-brown gelatinous precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide with NaOH, which remains insoluble even in excess of the alkali.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Adding sodium hydroxide solution to a solution containing Cu2+ ions produces
options: a pale blue gelatinous precipitate that is insoluble in excess NaOH
a white precipitate that is soluble in excess NaOH
a green precipitate that is soluble in excess NaOH
no precipitate, only a colour change of the solution
questions.explanation: Cu2+ ions form a pale blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide with NaOH, which persists (does not redissolve) even when excess NaOH is added.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Adding sodium hydroxide solution dropwise, then in excess, to a solution containing Zn2+ ions produces
options: a reddish-brown precipitate that is insoluble in excess NaOH
a white precipitate that remains insoluble in excess NaOH
a blue precipitate that is insoluble in excess NaOH
a white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH to form a colourless solution
questions.explanation: Zn2+ forms an amphoteric white precipitate, zinc hydroxide, which dissolves in excess NaOH to form a soluble, colourless zincate complex, distinguishing it from Ca2+ or Fe ions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Adding sodium hydroxide solution dropwise, then in excess, to a solution containing Al3+ ions produces
options: a reddish-brown precipitate that is soluble in excess NaOH
a green precipitate that is insoluble in excess NaOH
a white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH to form a colourless solution
a white precipitate that remains insoluble in excess NaOH
questions.explanation: Al3+ forms an amphoteric white precipitate, aluminium hydroxide, which redissolves in excess NaOH to give a colourless aluminate solution, just like Zn2+.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Adding sodium hydroxide solution to a solution containing Ca2+ ions produces
options: no precipitate is formed at all
a blue precipitate that is insoluble in excess NaOH
a white precipitate that dissolves readily in excess NaOH
a white precipitate that remains insoluble even in excess NaOH
questions.explanation: Ca2+ gives a white precipitate of calcium hydroxide with NaOH (though only slightly soluble overall), and unlike Zn2+ or Al3+, this precipitate does not dissolve in excess alkali.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Adding sodium hydroxide solution and gently warming a solution containing NH4+ (ammonium) ions produces
options: no precipitate, but a pungent gas is released that turns moist red litmus paper blue
a white precipitate that is insoluble in excess NaOH
a green precipitate that dissolves on warming
a reddish-brown precipitate that dissolves on warming
questions.explanation: NH4+ ions do not form a precipitate with NaOH; instead, warming releases ammonia gas, identifiable by its pungent smell and its ability to turn moist red litmus paper blue.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Adding aqueous ammonia dropwise, then in excess, to a solution containing Cu2+ ions produces
options: a reddish-brown precipitate insoluble in excess ammonia
a white precipitate that dissolves in excess ammonia
a pale blue precipitate that remains insoluble in excess ammonia
a pale blue precipitate that dissolves in excess ammonia to form a deep blue solution
questions.explanation: Cu2+ first forms a pale blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide with a little ammonia, which then dissolves in excess ammonia to form the characteristic deep blue tetraamminecopper(II) complex.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which observation confirms the presence of the trioxocarbonate(IV) ion, CO3 2-, in a solid sample?
options: Effervescence with dilute acid, producing a gas that turns limewater milky
A brown ring forms when the solid is mixed with iron(II) sulphate and concentrated sulphuric acid
A pungent gas that turns moist red litmus blue is released
A white precipitate forms immediately on adding water
questions.explanation: Carbonates react with dilute acids to effervesce, releasing carbon dioxide gas, which is confirmed by its ability to turn freshly prepared limewater milky (a white precipitate of CaCO3).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which test confirms the presence of the sulphate(VI) ion, SO4 2-, in solution?
options: Adding acidified potassium heptaoxodichromate(VI) decolourises it
Adding silver nitrate gives a yellow precipitate
Adding barium chloride gives a white precipitate that dissolves readily in dilute hydrochloric acid
Adding dilute hydrochloric acid followed by barium chloride solution gives a white precipitate that is insoluble in the acid
questions.explanation: Sulphate ions form a white precipitate of barium sulphate with barium chloride that, crucially, does not dissolve in dilute hydrochloric acid, distinguishing SO4 2- from SO3 2-.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which observation distinguishes the sulphate(IV) ion (sulphite, SO3 2-) from the sulphate(VI) ion (sulphate, SO4 2-) when barium chloride is added?
options: The sulphate gives a yellow precipitate while the sulphite gives a white one
The sulphite gives no precipitate at all with barium chloride
The sulphite gives a white precipitate that dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid, while the sulphate's precipitate does not
Both give precipitates that dissolve equally in dilute hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: Both ions form white barium precipitates, but barium sulphite (unlike barium sulphate) readily dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid, releasing sulphur dioxide gas, providing the distinguishing test.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which test confirms the presence of the chloride ion, Cl-, in solution?
options: Adding iron(II) sulphate and concentrated sulphuric acid gives a brown ring
Adding dilute nitric acid followed by silver nitrate solution gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess aqueous ammonia
Adding barium chloride solution gives a white precipitate insoluble in dilute hydrochloric acid
Adding acidified potassium heptaoxodichromate(VI) turns the solution green
questions.explanation: Chloride ions form a white precipitate of silver chloride with acidified silver nitrate solution, and this precipitate characteristically dissolves in excess aqueous ammonia, unlike silver bromide or silver iodide.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The brown ring test, in which a solution containing iron(II) sulphate is carefully layered with concentrated sulphuric acid, is used to confirm the presence of which ion?
questions.explanation: The brown ring test is a classic confirmatory test for the nitrate ion: a brown ring of an iron-nitroso complex forms at the interface where the concentrated acid layer meets the iron(II) sulphate solution.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which observation confirms the identity of hydrogen gas?
options: It burns with a squeaky pop sound when a lit splint is introduced
It bleaches moist blue litmus paper
questions.explanation: Hydrogen gas is confirmed by the distinctive 'pop' sound produced when it combusts rapidly with oxygen in air on contact with a lit splint.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which observation confirms the identity of oxygen gas?
options: It gives a brown ring with iron(II) sulphate
It turns moist red litmus paper blue
questions.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion vigorously, so introducing a glowing (not flaming) splint into a test tube of the gas causes the splint to burst back into flame.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which observation confirms the identity of carbon dioxide gas?
options: It turns freshly prepared limewater milky
It burns with a pop sound
It turns moist red litmus paper blue
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) to form an insoluble white precipitate of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV), turning the limewater milky/cloudy.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which set of observations confirms the identity of ammonia gas?
options: It bleaches moist litmus paper and has a choking smell
It is colourless, odourless, and relights a glowing splint
It has a pungent smell, turns moist red litmus paper blue, and produces dense white fumes with hydrogen chloride gas
It gives a brown ring test with iron(II) sulphate
questions.explanation: Ammonia is a pungent, alkaline gas; it turns moist red litmus blue, and reacts with hydrogen chloride gas/fumes to form dense white fumes of solid ammonium chloride.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which observation confirms the identity of chlorine gas?
options: It has a rotten-egg smell and turns lead ethanoate paper black
It is a colourless gas that relights a glowing splint
It gives dense white fumes when mixed with ammonia gas near the gas jar mouth without any colour of its own
It is a greenish-yellow gas with a pungent smell that bleaches moist litmus paper
questions.explanation: Chlorine is a characteristic greenish-yellow, choking, pungent gas that first turns moist blue litmus paper red and then rapidly bleaches it white due to its strong oxidising action.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which observation confirms the identity of hydrogen chloride gas?
options: It produces dense white fumes when it meets ammonia gas, and turns moist blue litmus paper red
questions.explanation: Hydrogen chloride gas is acidic (turning moist blue litmus red) and reacts with ammonia vapour to produce dense white fumes of solid ammonium chloride, a classic identification test.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which observation confirms the identity of sulphur(IV) oxide (sulphur dioxide) gas?
options: It turns moist red litmus paper blue
It decolourises acidified potassium heptaoxodichromate(VI) solution, turning it from orange to green
It produces a squeaky pop with a lit splint
questions.explanation: Sulphur dioxide is a reducing agent that decolourises acidified potassium heptaoxodichromate(VI) (dichromate) solution, changing its colour from orange to green, a standard confirmatory test.
